outcome: Nothing has settled the divisibility conjecture as stated since 26 January 2024, and I found no peer-reviewed or independently checked progress. The one in-window event that claims to move it is a March 2024 unrefereed Preprints.org preprint (C. Hannusch) asserting the non-divisibility for twin-prime pairs p = q+2; I could not open the preprint, found no review, citation or journal version, and did not read the proof. The other in-window items concern the stronger coprimality form (a 2025 counterexample search that found nothing new) or namesake problems.
problem_asks: For every pair of distinct primes p and q: the number (p^q - 1)/(p - 1) does not divide (q^p - 1)/(q - 1). This is one universal negative divisibility claim over all pairs of distinct primes. Because the quantifier ranges over all ordered pairs, each unordered pair {p, q} is covered in both directions. The statement does not ask for the stronger form that the two quotients are always coprime (gcd > 1 never occurs), which is a different claim and is refuted by Stephens (1971) with p = 17, q = 3313.

events.what_happened: NAMESAKE ONLY, NOT THIS QUESTION. W. Feit and J. G. Thompson, 'Solvability of groups of odd order', Pacific J. Math. 13 (1963), 775-1029: every finite group of odd order is solvable. The conjecture was motivated by this proof: if the divisibility claim held, the final chapter would be shortened. A Coq formalisation of the odd-order theorem exists (search results cite a 2012 announcement and ITP 2013; the Lean eval page cites the Coq work and says there is no Lean port). Recorded so the namesake is visible to the judging pass; it settles nothing about the divisibility claim.
events.delivers: Solvability of finite groups of odd order. A different problem sharing the names Feit and Thompson. Delivers nothing about primes p, q or the quotients (p^q - 1)/(p - 1).
events.remains: The whole of the divisibility claim.

checked_by.qualification: Machine-checked formal proof project; a human-led project reported via the Lean eval page and search results
checked_by.what_they_did: Formalised the odd-order theorem in Coq (not reached directly; package page seen in search results only)

events.time_since_posted: 63 years for the theorem; not applicable to the conjecture
events.direction: Not applicable: a different theorem sharing the namesakes. It does not cut for or against the divisibility claim.

events.what_happened: N. M. Stephens, 'On the Feit-Thompson Conjecture', Mathematics of Computation 25(115), p. 625 (July 1971; DOI 10.2307/2005226). By computer search Stephens found p = 17, q = 3313 for which the two quotients share the factor 2pq + 1 = 112643, which refutes the stronger coprimality form. Wikipedia also cites this paper for the case q = 2 of the divisibility claim. The paper itself was not reachable (AMS PDF returned 403). The content above comes from secondary sources: ProofWiki, Groupprops, MathWorld, Wikipedia, and Motose 2012 (which opens by saying Stephens found the example for 17 and 3313).
events.delivers: Refutes only the stronger form (the two quotients are always coprime), which is not what the statement asks. Per Wikipedia, establishes the divisibility claim for q = 2. Checked independently by me: for q = 2 and odd p, (p^2 - 1)/(p - 1) = p + 1 is even while (2^p - 1)/1 = 2^p - 1 is odd, so p + 1 cannot divide it, and 2^p - 1 exceeds p + 1, so the reverse divisibility fails too. The q = 2 case is elementary.
events.remains: On the Wikipedia reading, every pair in which neither prime is 2. On the stricter reading that the paper says nothing about divisibility, everything. The coprime form is not part of the statement.

checked_by.qualification: Author of several papers on this conjecture, published in the refereed Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A
checked_by.what_they_did: Re-derived the Stephens primes 17 and 3313 as common index divisors of cyclotomic subfields using the Artin map (2012)

events.directly_checkable: The pair p = 17, q = 3313: the claimed common factor 2pq + 1 = 2 x 17 x 3313 + 1 = 112643 checks by hand (I did this arithmetic). Whether 112643 divides both quotients is a finite computation I did not run (Bash approval was refused). For q = 2 the case is checkable by hand as above.
events.direction: Against the stronger coprime form: it is a counterexample to coprimality. Against the divisibility claim as stated in the bullet: no counterexample; the divisibility claim is not refuted. For q = 2 it supports the conjecture (per Wikipedia, and by my parity check).
events.object: The pair p = 17, q = 3313. The two quotients (p^q - 1)/(p - 1) and (q^p - 1)/(q - 1) share the common factor 112643 = 2pq + 1. This is an explicit computer-found pair, not a non-constructive existence result. It is a counterexample to coprimality, not to divisibility. ProofWiki says the search covered p < 443, pq < 200000 and r < 400000; MathWorld reports no other such pair with both values below 400000.

events.what_happened: Kaoru Motose, 'Notes to the Feit-Thompson conjecture', Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A 85(2), 16-17 (February 2009; DOI 10.3792/pjaa.85.16). The abstract (opened) reads: 'We shall present partial solutions to the conjecture such that (q^p-1)/(q-1) does not divide (p^q-1)/(p-1) for distinct primes p<q.' Its full text is behind a subscription and I could not read it, so which (p, q) cases are proved is unknown to me.
events.delivers: Partial solutions of the divisibility claim, written for p < q as (q^p-1)/(q-1) not dividing (p^q-1)/(p-1). Since p and q range over all distinct primes, this is the bullet's claim in one direction for each pair. Which restricted cases are established is not visible from the abstract.
events.remains: Not determinable from the abstract. The general claim is open on every source I read.

checked_by.who: Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A (refereed journal)

events.direction: Partial results in favour of the divisibility claim (no counterexample is reported).

events.what_happened: Kaoru Motose, 'Notes to the Feit-Thompson conjecture. II', Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A 86(8), 131-132 (October 2010; DOI 10.3792/pjaa.86.131). The abstract (opened) states the conjecture for distinct primes p < q and says the paper 'is a record on partial solutions to this conjecture for small primes 3 and 5'. Keywords: Eisenstein reciprocity, odd order theorem, power residue symbol. A search excerpt quoting the paper (I did not open the full text) reports the reduction that if q is congruent to 1 mod p then the quotient (p^q-1)/(p-1) is 1 mod p while (q^p-1)/(q-1) is 0 mod p, so the claim holds, and the paper therefore assumes q not congruent to 1 mod p.
events.delivers: Partial solutions for the small primes p = 3 and p = 5 (per the abstract), i.e. the claim with one of the primes fixed at 3 or 5 and the other arbitrary, subject to conditions I could not read in full. The congruence reduction (q = 1 mod p settles the case) is from the search excerpt, not from a page I opened.
events.remains: Every pair in which neither prime is 3 or 5, and whatever residual conditions the paper leaves for p = 3 and 5.

checked_by.who: Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A (refereed journal)

events.direction: Partial results in favour of the divisibility claim for p = 3 and p = 5 (no counterexample).

events.what_happened: Le Mao-hua (also written Le Maohua), '[A divisibility problem concerning group theory]', 2012, cited by Wikipedia as Pure Appl. Math. Q. for the case q = 3 of the divisibility claim. I did not reach the paper. A search returned only a garbled bibliographic listing with a 2012 entry under Le Mao-hua. The title in brackets is my reconstruction from that listing and is unverified; the listing also records a 2006 Le paper on a related divisibility, which is a different result.
events.delivers: Per Wikipedia: the divisibility claim for q = 3, i.e. pairs in which 3 is one of the primes. Unverified against the paper.
events.remains: Every pair in which neither prime is 3. The q = 2 case is elementary (see stephens-1971).
events.time_since_posted: about 14 years; the only public mention I found is Wikipedia's citation
events.direction: In favour of the divisibility claim for q = 3 (no counterexample), if Wikipedia's statement is accurate.

events.what_happened: Kaoru Motose, 'The example by Stephens', Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A 88(3), 35-37 (DOI 10.3792/pjaa.88.35; first online 5 March 2012). The abstract (opened) reads: 'Concerning the Feit-Thompson conjecture, Stephens found an example for primes 17 and 3313. In this paper, using the Artin map, these primes are common index divisors of subfields of a cyclotomic field, and some results in [7,8] shall be again proved.' The paper concerns the stronger coprime form's counterexample. Its full text was not reachable.
events.delivers: A structural explanation of the 17/3313 counterexample to the coprime form (common index divisors of cyclotomic subfields). It establishes nothing about the divisibility claim.
events.remains: The whole of the divisibility claim.

checked_by.who: Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. A (refereed journal)

events.direction: Neutral for the divisibility claim. Bears only on the coprime counterexample.

events.what_happened: C. Hannusch (the author's publication page shows C. Hannusch; a ResearchGate URL gives Carolin Hannusch), 'The Feit-Thompson Conjecture: An Example for Mathematical Research Based on Contradictory Sources', Preprints.org, DOI 10.20944/preprints202403.1214.v1, posted March 2024 (manuscript ID 202403). The author's own publication page lists it as a Preprints.org preprint with no journal version. Preprints.org and ResearchGate both returned HTTP 403 when I tried to open them, so the abstract wording below is from search-result excerpts, not from a page I opened. Excerpt: 'Thus we prove that the Feit-Thompson conjecture is true for twin prime numbers', where twin primes means p = q+2. The excerpt also says the paper has a second aim, to resolve contradictions among online sources about the conjecture, and marks the version as not peer-reviewed with zero comments at crawl time. Only v1 was seen.
events.revisions: Only v1 seen (March 2024). No later version found.
events.delivers: Claims that (p^q-1)/(p-1) does not divide (q^p-1)/(q-1) when p and q are twin primes, p = q+2. This is a restricted case: the family of twin-prime pairs only. The proof was not read by me. On the author's own description it is a proof for twin primes, not a general result.
events.remains: Every pair of distinct primes that is not a twin pair (p = q+2), which is the bulk of the claim.
events.directly_checkable: Small twin pairs can be checked by hand, which tests the statement but not the proof: (p,q) = (5,3) gives 31 and 121, and 31 does not divide 121; (p,q) = (7,5) gives 2801 and 19531, and 2801 does not divide 19531. These are my own arithmetic. The twin-prime proof itself has not been checked by anyone I could find.
events.direction: If the proof holds, it cuts for the conjecture on twin-prime pairs (no divisibility occurs there). It claims a special case and does not address the general claim.
people: Carolin Hannusch (C. Hannusch on the author's page)

A publisher link in search results points to the Journal of the European Mathematical Society (DOI 10.4171/jems/1742); not opened. Recorded so the namesake is visible.

events.what_happened: NAMESAKE ONLY, NOT THIS QUESTION. Jun Liao, Lizhong Wang and Jiping Zhang, 'Thompson's Conjecture for Finite Simple Groups of Lie Type over Small Fields', arXiv:2608.17891 (math.GR, math.RT; submitted 18 August 2026; 69 pages). The abstract (opened) says the paper proves that every finite simple group of Lie type over a field of order at most 8 has a conjugacy class whose square is the whole group, completing Thompson's conjecture in that setting. This is Thompson's conjugacy-class problem, not the Feit-Thompson prime-divisibility claim. A search-result summary (not from the paper) said the authors used ChatGPT to explore proof strategies. The PDF was unreadable to me, so I could not confirm that statement. Recorded as a namesake; the AI statement, if true, concerns another problem.
events.delivers: Thompson's conjugacy-class squares problem for finite simple groups of Lie type over fields of order at most 8. A different problem.
events.remains: The whole of the divisibility claim.

disputes.summary: MathWorld says the Stephens example (p = 17, q = 3313, common factor 112643) shows the conjecture 'is, in fact, false'. ProofWiki, Wikipedia and Groupprops attribute the refutation to the stronger coprime form and keep the divisibility claim as a conjecture. I follow the latter reading: a common factor of the two quotients does not divide one into the other, so the example does not refute the divisibility claim.

ProofWiki (per a search-result excerpt of its historical note; not opened directly) says David Wells, in The Penguin Dictionary of Curious and Interesting Numbers (1986), misreports the Stephens result as a statement about the common divisor of p^q - 1 and q^p - 1 rather than about the quotients.

summary: Since 26 January 2024 the divisibility conjecture has not been settled, and no event in the window moves it in a way I could verify. The one in-window event that claims to move it is C. Hannusch's Preprints.org preprint of March 2024 (DOI 10.20944/preprints202403.1214.v1), which asserts non-divisibility for twin-prime pairs p = q+2. Preprints.org and ResearchGate both returned 403, so its wording is taken from search-result excerpts of its abstract and from the author's own publication page, which lists it as an unrefereed preprint with no journal version. I found no review, rebuttal, citation, or later version, and I did not read the proof. The pre-window record consists of restricted cases. Stephens (1971) refuted the stronger coprime form with p = 17, q = 3313 (common factor 2pq + 1 = 112643, which I checked arithmetically), and per Wikipedia also proved the q = 2 case, which I confirmed is elementary by parity (p + 1 is even while 2^p - 1 is odd). Le (2012), per Wikipedia, proved the q = 3 case; I did not reach the paper, only a garbled listing and Wikipedia's citation. Motose (2009) gave partial solutions for p < q whose exact cases I could not read; Motose (2010) gave partial solutions for p = 3 and p = 5 (abstract read); Motose (2012) reproved the Stephens example via the Artin map and does not touch the divisibility claim. The statement quantifies over all ordered pairs of distinct primes, so Motose's p < q form is the same claim. Current Wikipedia (last edited 10 May 2026 per the fetched page) lists only q = 2 and q = 3 as known cases. The 2025 puzzle-site searches (Branicky up to p<q<=31627; Izquierdo; Heleen) concern only the coprime form and found nothing beyond (17, 3313). Liao, Wang and Zhang (arXiv 2608.17891, August 2026) prove a different 'Thompson's conjecture' on squares of conjugacy classes and are recorded as a namesake; a search summary said they used ChatGPT, but the PDF was unreadable to me, so I could not confirm it, and it concerns another problem. AI: no source I could read names an AI system in connection with this conjecture. I checked the 2026 lab releases most likely to reach it. OpenAI's Astra announcement (1 August 2026; the ten results listed on TheNextWeb and the ten-proofs repository) includes nothing on this conjecture. OpenAI's manuscript repository (github.com/openai/math, 6 October 2026) states 719 manuscripts in 372 families; its README shows titles only for reasoning summaries, none matching, and the full catalogue CONTENTS.md was unreadable, so an unlisted manuscript cannot be excluded. DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus preprint (arXiv 2605.22763) showed no mention in the abstract view, which is not a full-text check. The Kourovka Notebook lists this as problem 4.65 (J. G. Thompson). The 20th edition (2022) has no comment on it in the retrieved text; I could not check the 21st edition (2026), and the arXiv listing (arXiv:1401.0300, v48, 6 October 2026) does not mention it in the fetched view. A Lean statement with sorry exists in the Benchify/BuddenBench dataset; it is a statement only and undated, so I did not record it as an event. On names: one search summary called the author 'Christian' Hannusch, but the author's own page shows 'C. Hannusch' and the ResearchGate URL 'Carolin Hannusch', so I used Carolin with that caveat. The computer searches (Stephens 1971; the 2025 puzzle-site searches) are computer-assisted, not AI.
competing_reading: Read as a case settled since the window opened, the Hannusch preprint is the only in-window event that moves the claim: it establishes non-divisibility for every twin-prime pair, a family the statement quantifies over, and a judging pass could count it as a restricted case. Against this: the claim is unrefereed, I found no one who has checked it, I did not read the proof, and twin-prime pairs are a thin family among all prime pairs. The same logic applies to the pre-window fixed-prime cases (q = 2 and q = 3 via Stephens and Le; p = 3 and p = 5 via Motose), which are restricted cases of the same kind. The q = 2 case is elementary, and the Le and Motose results are not read in full. A reading that counts none of these as movement treats them as finite or fixed-prime instances of a universal claim, which the bullet's own wording does not exclude.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Hannusch's preprint and its proof, especially the step where twin primes are used; any referee report or journal version; any citing paper. (2) The full text of Le (2012): the exact statement, whether 'q = 3' covers both divisibility directions, and the journal. (3) The full text of Motose 2009 and 2010: exactly which (p, q) cases are proved. (4) Stephens (1971): whether it says anything about q = 2 or about divisibility. (5) The Kourovka Notebook 21st edition (2026) entry for problem 4.65, and any comment on it. (6) MathOverflow question 63233 'Variant of Stephens result' (blocked to me). (7) OpenAI's CONTENTS.md or the full list of 719 manuscripts, to rule out an AI-derived case of this conjecture; a full-text check of the Astra manuscript for the name. (8) A zbMATH or MathSciNet search for later citations of Motose or Le, and for any post-2024 review of the Hannusch preprint.
